keyNumbers.note: 2026 forecasts: ~0.14 (BIMCO) to over 0.4 (Drewry), revised down. Ships over 25 years: ~1.6 M TEU (BIMCO).

speakerNotes: Sanjoy, about 3.5 min. Step 0: the framework (three groups of measures, four objectives). Steps 1-5 in the order of his ppt.pdf: fleet management, slow steaming (fuel bars: say 'illustrative'), scrapping (lay-up vs scrapping), network design (Gemini example), consolidation, close on the four objectives. Gemini figures from Lloyd's List / Kuehne+Nagel at launch, unverified.
headline: How can carriers respond to overcapacity?

responses.title: Fleet management
responses.line: Adjust vessel deployment and charter commitments.
points: Fleet redeployment: shift vessels towards routes with stronger cargo demand
Charter adjustment: reduce chartered capacity when contracts permit
Lay-up: temporarily withdraw vessels from active service
Vessel-size adjustment: match deployed capacity to route demand
Enough total capacity can still mean an imbalance on single routes

responses.title: Slow steaming
responses.line: Reduce speed to absorb effective capacity and save fuel.
points: Fuel use rises steeply with speed (simplified cube rule)
Slower rotations absorb excess capacity: ships take longer per loop
Trade-off: slower voyages can require additional vessels to maintain weekly service frequency

fuel.title: Illustrative fuel consumption comparison
fuel.sub: Simplified Cube Rule; 16 knots is the baseline.
fuel.note: Illustrative calculation, not a measured fleet-wide result. Actual consumption depends on vessel characteristics, weather, engine load and operating conditions.

responses.title: Scrapping
responses.line: Permanently remove older vessels, to reduce fleet supply.
points: Owner offers the ship, a broker circulates it, demolition buyers bid, the yard recycles it
Scrap value = lightweight tonnage × scrap price per LWT
Limits: owners keep ships that still pay, and newbuilds offset the removals

compare.l: Temporary withdrawal. The vessel can return to service.
Permanent removal from the commercial fleet.

responses.title: Network design
responses.line: Optimise routes, port calls and vessel allocation.
points: Optimise routes, service loops and port rotations
Match vessel size and frequency to cargo demand
Improve vessel utilisation and operational efficiency

example.title: Example: Gemini Cooperation, Maersk + Hapag-Lloyd (since Feb 2025)
points: Hub-and-spoke: mainliners call at a few hub ports, shuttles feed the regional ports
57 services at launch: 29 mainliners and 28 shuttles, about 340 ships, 3.7 M TEU
Target: over 90% schedule reliability
example.source: Lloyd’s List and Kuehne+Nagel (Jan 2025); Hapag-Lloyd Gemini page. Shuttle count differs by source (28 or 29).

responses.title: Consolidation
responses.line: Combine overlapping services and coordinate capacity.
points: Combine overlapping or underutilised services and reduce duplicated capacity
Coordinate vessel deployment between carriers, keep transit times and reliability
Example: Hapag-Lloyd and Maersk's Gemini Cooperation (2025)
responses.close: Managing overcapacity is not simply about removing ships. Carriers balance four goals: better utilisation, cost control, reliable services and profitability.

top.s: Fleet capacity grows faster than cargo demand

goals.s: Better utilisation · Cost control · Reliable services · Profitability
